items.title: Clark Terry interviewed by Joe Williams and Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, May 19, 1995
items.q: That thing, and the other side too, “The Comeback.” Foster wrote that.

ctx.x: That thing, and the other side too, “The Comeback.” Foster wrote that. Everybody stole from that.

items.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Was it Frank Foster or whatever. Before any of them were considered, they asked me.

ctx.x: When the – when Basie passed, did you want to run that band? Or was it not . . .

At one point I was asked to front the band, and I was up for consideration. This was before Thad [Jones] or Joe Williams or any of the cats that took over. Was it Frank Foster or whatever. Before any of them were considered, they asked me. Norman Granz was on the board, and Norman vetoed. He said, “No. I will not allow him to do that.” I said – somebody called him Smedley – I said, “Smedley, why did you not want me?” He said, “Because you’d be dead in a year’s time.” So I suppose I have to thank Smedley for not…
How did Norman Granz get the nickname Smitty?

items.title: Frank Foster interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 7, 1998
items.q: performing and recording with a long list of top jazz artists, including Elvin Jones and Clark Terry.

ctx.x: Frank Foster is one of the most skilled and versatile jazz veterans working today. He was born in Cincinnati, Ohio, on September 23, 1928 and was leading and writing charts for a 12-piece band while still in high school. Frank honed his saxophone playing with Snooky Young and Milt Jackson and became a part of the “New Testament” Count Basie Orchestra immediately after military service. His original work penned for the Basie band was a huge part of their success as was his sharing of the tenor sax solos with…
Frank was interviewed in Clinton, NY on April 7, 1998, by Monk Rowe, director of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive.
